newsitem.title: MALI: Mali opposition slams planned election law change.
newsitem.headline: Mali opposition slams planned election law change.

text.p: Mali's 12 main opposition parties held a protest meeting on Sunday to denounce a government plan to change electoral law ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections due in the first half of 1997.
Party representatives met for three hours and outlined their objections to the plan, which envisages an independent electoral commission and a mixed system of voting for parliament.

Professor Mamadou Kassa Traore of the Movement for African Independence, Rebirth and Integration, which broke away from President Alpha Oumar Konare's ADEMA party, said the meeting showed the opposition could unite.
"The fact we have held this meeting in spite of the predictions proves the opposition parties can unite," he said.
He accused Konare, elected during the 1992 democratic transition, of "abusing the trust of the masses" and ADEMA, his Alliance for Democracy in Mali, of "anti-democratic behaviour".
ADEMA won an outright majority in the 116-seat parliament in 1992 elections. Parliament has yet to vote on the election law.
The cabinet in August approved a draft law envisaging a 30-member electoral commission to oversee the elections.

Under the draft, Mali would continue to elect a president by simple majority but in parliamentary elections larger districts returning four or more deputies would elect them by simple majority, smaller districts would use a proportional system.

Former dictator Moussa Traore was toppled from power in a mass uprising in 1991. Lieutenant-Colonel Amadou Toumani Toure ran the West African country for 15 months, stepping down after Konare won multi-party elections.
